newsitem.title: USA: Talks reset for Saturday after N. Korea stays away.
newsitem.headline: Talks reset for Saturday after N. Korea stays away.

text.p: North Korea failed to resume talks with the United States and South Korea on Friday on a landmark peace proposal, forcing the meeting to be delayed until Saturday.

The talks were called to hear Pyongyang's formal response to a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.
U.S. and South Korean officials remained hopeful the North would respond positively.

The talks, adjourned after an inconclusive day-long meeting on Wednesday, were to resume on Friday morning at 10 a.m. EDT (1400 GMT) at a Manhattan hotel. U.S. officials said they were told by the North Koreans they were awaiting direction from Pyongyang.
The American and South Korean teams waited all day until a decision was made in early evening to reschedule for Saturday.

The South Korean delegation planned to leave New York for Seoul on Friday night. But Yu Myung-hwan, director general of the foreign ministry's North American affairs bureau, told reporters the team decided to stay through Saturday.
"It is my personal judgment that it may not be possible to have a meeting today," Yu said, adding: "Still I have some hope that we can strike a deal by tomorrow."
Another South Korean official, Ji Won Suh, expressed frustration, saying "this is not a game." He said he was suspicious of North Korea's claim to be consulting with Pyongyang.
Later, after the postponement was agreed, Ji laughed when asked if he felt assured the North Koreans would show up on Saturday.

"How anybody could say this (delay) is desirable? But it is mutually beneficial to give (your) counterpart maximum time," Ji said. He stressed, however, "we have our limits" and U.S. officials also indicated they would not wait in New York indefinitely for Pyongyang's reply.

A spokesman for North Korea's mission to the United Nations, who declined to be identified, told Reuters after his country's team failed to arrive for the Friday morning session on time: "We need to contact with capitals."
Asked if there was a problem, he said: "I cannot say anything in connection with that."
U.S. officials said privately Pyongyang essentially accepted the peace talks proposal on Wednesday but then tied its acceptance to demands for additional food assistance.
On Thursday, however, U.S. officials ruled out the possibility Washington or Seoul would announce new food aid before Pyongyang conclusively answered the peace proposal.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns denied this might be why North Korea postponed Friday's talks. He shrugged off the delay, saying "this kind of thing happens all the time in negotiations."

The three delegations opened Wednesday's meeting with optimistic statements and an apparent warmth and conviviality. Later, they all reported progress and said they hoped to settle the issue when they resumed on Friday.
Pyongyang's Stalinist regime has been preoccupied with increasingly severe food shortages caused by two years of floods, insisting on more and more international help.
After some skepticism in Washington and elsewhere, it has been widely accepted that impoverished Stalinist North Korea is facing a serious problem that could reach famine stage by June.
North Korea and independent experts say the country needs 2.3 million tons of food this year.
The U.N. World Food Program recently appealed for 200,000 metric tons of food, with Washington offering one-quarter of that amount, including a $15 million contribution on Monday.
But U.S. officials have said Pyongyang cannot expect massive assistance until it enters peace talks and begins to defuse tensions on the volatile Korean peninsula.
Peace talks, if accepted by Pyongyang, may not begin until June or July. China would be the fourth participant.
